ms-sos-sample-ballot-2026.title: Sample ballot, November 3, 2026 general election (dated September 9, 2026)

n.t: No statewide question is on the November 3, 2026 ballot in Mississippi. The Secretary of State's statewide sample ballot for the election lists offices only. Mississippi's initiative process has had no working path since the state Supreme Court's 2021 ruling, and the Legislature put no amendment on this ballot.
Local questions (bonds, alcohol sales, school questions) are called by counties and cities and printed on their own ballots; the state keeps no list. They are not shown here yet.

g.r: There is no statewide list; each county's circuit clerk and each city clerk posts its own.

methods: Who is running comes only from the Mississippi Secretary of State’s own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local races are not loaded for Mississippi yet; they are loaded for 39 states so far, shown on the states page.

What is read. From those lists this site reads only the office, the district, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one. Addresses, phone numbers, e-mail and websites, where a list carries them, are never read, kept or shown. No photos, ages, biographies or campaign money are shown for state candidates.
Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out. Judges are on the nonpartisan ballot; the page says so instead of a party.
Order. Candidates appear in the ballot order the list gives, or by surname where it gives none. Never by money, polls or party.

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page and nothing more.

Maps and “use my location”. District lines are the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files (2024 Census Bureau cartographic boundary files), the lines the state pages draw; your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your district. Your location is worked out on your own device and never sent anywhere; a rounded copy (about half a mile) is kept on the device, with your choices, until you tap “Forget”. A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address.
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from the Census Bureau’s 119th Congress lines, the ones the Congress pages draw, on your own device.

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: The Senate's hours without its recesses, like the House's
items: The Senate's hours on the floor now leave out its recesses too. The count with them is shown beside it, as for the House.

The Senate's daily summary in the Congressional Record does not list its recesses, so they are read from the Senate's own pages of the Record: "the Senate, at 12:31 p.m., recessed until 2:15 p.m." A recess is counted to the time set for the Senate to reassemble, unless the Record gives another time.
Checked against the Record's own count for 2025: 1,266 hours 9 minutes here and 1,265 hours 21 minutes in the Record.
Each Senate day's details now show its recesses.

changelog.title: The calendar: hours without the breaks, and votes on the Congress home
items: Hours on the floor now leave out the recesses the Congressional Record lists. The count with the recesses is shown beside it, and each day's details show both.
The Senate's Daily Digest does not list its recesses, so the Senate's hours still include them. The tile says so.
Two House days in 2025 have a recess printed with times that cannot fall inside that day's meeting. Those recesses are shown as printed and nothing is taken out for them.

March 27, 2026 is now read correctly. That day the House ended its sitting by voting on a motion to adjourn, then met again in the evening. The fix adds about 3 House hours not counting recesses, or 12 counting them.
The Senate's count of planned days called off now says on the tile that it goes by whole weeks, because the Senate's schedule does not name the days it will meet.
The calendar tiles on the Congress home now include each chamber's recorded votes.
The spreadsheet download has a new column: minutes on the floor, not counting recesses.

changelog.title: The calendar of Congress
items: New page, Calendar, beside What's moving and Coming up: every day of this Congress, House and Senate apart, from January 3, 2025, with each chamber's published plans ahead to January 3, 2027.
Each day shows what the Congressional Record says: a full session, a pro forma session (a short meeting with no business expected) or no meeting, with the times the chamber convened and adjourned.

Beside it, the chamber's own calendar. A day the House's calendar had as a voting day, when the Record shows only a pro forma session or no meeting, is listed as called off. The Senate's schedule lists only the weeks it plans to be away, so a Senate day is listed as called off only when a whole planned week passed with no full session. The page links the calendar, the Record and anything posted about the day. It does not say why.

Four tiles for each chamber: days in session (full and pro forma counted apart), planned days called off and weekdays of scheduled time away, hours on the floor, and recorded votes (every roll call in each chamber's own list, nominations included).

The page checks itself against the Record's own table for 2025: the same 202 days in session for the Senate and the same vote totals for both chambers (659 and 361); where a figure differs, it says why.
Choose a chamber, the kinds of day, the months, a calendar or a list, or only days with recorded votes. Your choices go in the address, so a view can be shared.
Press any day for its details: the Record's own sentence with a link to its page, recesses, the plan, announcements, that day's recorded votes and what passed.
Download the days you are looking at as a spreadsheet. Sources and how we count, at the foot of the page, says where each part comes from and what the figures cannot tell you.
Small session tiles on the Congress home lead to the calendar. It is brought up to date with every Congress update.

changelog.title: Congress as it moves
items: Alerts for every step a bill takes: floor votes with each party's tally, a bill passing or failing, the other chamber's changes, a bill heading to the President, signed into law or vetoed, committee approvals, calendar placements and cosponsors. New bills and cosponsor changes come as one roundup a day.
A banner at the top of every page shows the big moments of the last twelve hours. "What's moving" lists everything, with filters for chamber, kind, topic, bills you follow and your members.
"Coming up" shows what the House and Senate have posted for their floors, with a countdown wherever a chamber posted a time, and Senate votes to end debate expected under the Senate's rules.

Follow a bill with its star, get alerts on this device with Notify me, set a reminder a day, an hour or 15 minutes before, and add a vote to your calendar or subscribe to one. Your choices stay on your device.

changelog.title: Each vote listed once
items: When the record lists the same vote twice in slightly different words, a bill's list of votes now shows it once, and "Start here" no longer counts it twice.

changelog.title: Veterans Day votes
items: The record of Congress now runs through Veterans Day, November 11, with the bills introduced this week.
The House passed the Take Care of America's Veterans Act (H.R. 9237) by voice vote, so no member-by-member tally was taken; it goes to the Senate next.

The Senate passed the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026 (H.R. 8552), this year's raise in disability compensation, without changes; having passed both chambers, it goes to the President.
The House also passed H.R. 1013 by 295 to 128, and ten more bills by voice vote. They lead the bill list, which opens with the latest floor votes.
